# Cell Architecture Studio

> Local-first, accessible 3D cell biology and neuroanatomy gallery with 12 schematic specimens, 90 mesh-mapped structures, 180 cited facts across 28 sources, and 2D membrane and action-potential simulators.

Registry version: 0.1.0. Totals: 12 specimens, 90/90 mesh-mapped structures, 180 cited facts, 28 sources, 1,047 procedural mesh instances, ~331,646 estimated triangles. Status: draft teaching content (12/12 biology reviews in draft; not medical advice). Content license: CC BY 4.0; code license: MIT.

## Interactive Views & Simulators

- **Explore (`/`)**: Browse all 12 specimens, inspect structures, read cited facts, and control the 3D scene.
- **Compare (`/compare`)**: Compare any two specimens side by side with two isolated 3D scene graphs, shared structure focus, and a 6-trait table.
- **Learn (`/learn`)**: Offline flashcards, 4-option quizzes, cited static Ask helper, and local IndexedDB v2 progress with export/delete.
- **Lab (`/lab`)**: Two 2D HTML5 canvas simulations that run without WebGL — Phospholipid bilayer self-assembly (313 molecules) and Action potential (voltage-gated Na+/K+ channels and myelinated saltatory conduction).
- **About (`/about`)**: Biology review status, CC BY 4.0 provenance, full source list, accessibility statement, and local privacy controls.

## Camera & Annotation Controls

- **OrbitControls**: Pointer drag orbit with damping (pan disabled, polar clamp 0.12π–0.88π, zoom distance 1.05–8.5).
- **Mesh / Focus**: Switch between full-specimen framing (`Mesh`) and bounding-box camera framing (`Focus`) on the selected structure via `CameraDirector`.
- **Cutaway**: Hides outer shell parts marked `cutawayHide` to reveal internal organelles or subcortical tracts.
- **Auto-rotate / Reset view / Save PNG**: Toggle gentle rotation (disabled when `prefers-reduced-motion` is enabled, paused on drag or hidden tab), reset camera to canonical framing, or export a PNG snapshot.
- **Raycast Picking & Keyboard List**: `PointerPicker` clicks in 3D synchronize two-way with the keyboard-accessible structure list and cited detail inspector (including mapping confidence, schematic notes, and a local copyable correction report).

## 3D Rendering Details

- **Engine**: Imperative Three.js (`@cas/viewer-core`) in a lazy-loaded chunk using `WebGLRenderer` (antialias, alpha, `preserveDrawingBuffer: true`, `SRGBColorSpace`, `ACESFilmicToneMapping` exposure `1.05`, pixel ratio <= 2) and `PerspectiveCamera` (38° FOV).
- **Lighting**: `PMREMGenerator` + `RoomEnvironment` IBL plus hemisphere, warm key, cool rim, and soft fill directional lights over a translucent circular stage.
- **Geometry**: 100% repository-authored procedural schematic geometry (27 primitives + deterministic seeded repeat patterns `scatter`, `shell`, `ring`, `line`, `helix`, `grid`). Every structural mesh carries an authored `structureId`. Previews (`/previews/*.svg`) are rendered deterministically from the same expanded instances.

## Specimens & Structures

### Plant cell (Elodea sp.)

- **Domain / Cell type**: plant · Mesophyll cell
- **Size & scale**: Typically tens of micrometres across — All geometry is schematic and unitless. No real-world scale is inferred from the model; the size note is a separate textbook range.
- **3D stats**: 77 mesh instances · ~20,344 estimated triangles · Capabilities: 3D procedural mesh, Structure camera focus, Cutaway shell toggle, Mesh-mapped highlighting, PNG screenshot export, GLB export capability · Preview: `/previews/plant-cell.svg`
- **Summary**: A photosynthetic plant cell: cellulose wall, large central vacuole, and chloroplasts pressed against the periphery.
- **Overview**: This schematic shows a mesophyll cell, the photosynthetic tissue inside a leaf. Unlike an animal cell, it is enclosed by a cellulose cell wall and usually dominated by a large central vacuole. Chloroplasts sit near the plasma membrane, where light and CO₂ are available. The model is illustrative: it does not represent cell size, organelle counts, or membrane ultrastructure to scale.
- **Traits**: Nucleus: Present | Cell wall: Cellulose primary wall | Chloroplasts: Present | Motility: Sessile; no cell crawling | Typical size: Tens of µm | Organisation: Eukaryotic, multicellular tissue
- **Structures (7)**:
  - **Cell wall** (high confidence; meshes: cell-wall, plasmodesma-0, plasmodesma-1, plasmodesma-2, plasmodesma-3, plasmodesma-4, plasmodesma-5): A rigid extracellular layer of cellulose microfibrils, hemicellulose, and pectin outside the plasma membrane. Function: Maintains cell shape, protects the cell, and resists turgor pressure so the cell does not take up water without limit.
    - Fact: Plant cell walls are built mainly from cellulose microfibrils embedded in a matrix that also contains hemicellulose and pectin. [OpenStax, §4.3, 'The Cell Wall' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-3-eukaryotic-cells)]
    - Fact: The cell wall maintains cell shape and helps prevent excessive water uptake. [OpenStax, §4.3, 'The Cell Wall' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-3-eukaryotic-cells)]
  - **Plasma membrane** (high confidence; meshes: plasma-membrane): A phospholipid bilayer with embedded proteins that sits just inside the cell wall and controls exchange with the environment. Function: Selectively regulates the movement of ions, water, and small molecules into and out of the cell.
    - Fact: The plasma membrane is a phospholipid bilayer containing proteins that regulate transport and signalling. [OpenStax, §4.3, 'The Plasma Membrane' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-3-eukaryotic-cells)]
    - Fact: In plant cells the plasma membrane lies between the cell wall and the cytoplasm. [National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI Bookshelf), Chapter 10, 'Membrane Structure' (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK21054/)]
  - **Central vacuole** (high confidence; meshes: central-vacuole): A large membrane-bound compartment that can occupy most of a mature plant cell's volume. Function: Stores water, ions, nutrients, and sometimes pigments or defensive compounds; its turgor pressure helps support the cell.
    - Fact: A mature plant cell's central vacuole may occupy as much as 90 percent of the cell's volume. [OpenStax, §4.3, 'Vacuoles' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-3-eukaryotic-cells)]
    - Fact: The vacuole is bounded by a membrane called the tonoplast. [OpenStax, §4.3, 'Vacuoles' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-3-eukaryotic-cells)]
  - **Nucleus** (high confidence; meshes: nucleus, nucleus-chromatin, nucleolus, nuclear-pore): The DNA-containing organelle, bounded by a double membrane and containing a dense nucleolus. Function: Stores most of the cell's genetic material and coordinates gene expression, growth, and division.
    - Fact: The nucleus is bounded by a nuclear envelope with pores and contains the cell's chromosomal DNA. [OpenStax, §4.3, 'The Nucleus' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-3-eukaryotic-cells)]
    - Fact: The nucleolus is the site of ribosomal RNA synthesis and ribosomal subunit assembly. [OpenStax, §4.3, 'The Nucleus' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-3-eukaryotic-cells)]
  - **Chloroplast** (high confidence; meshes: chloroplast-0, chloroplast-1, chloroplast-2, chloroplast-3, chloroplast-4, chloroplast-5, chloroplast-6, chloroplast-7, chloroplast-granum-a-0, chloroplast-granum-b-0, chloroplast-lamella-0, chloroplast-granum-a-1, chloroplast-granum-b-1, chloroplast-lamella-1, chloroplast-granum-a-2, chloroplast-granum-b-2, chloroplast-lamella-2, chloroplast-granum-a-3, chloroplast-granum-b-3, chloroplast-lamella-3, chloroplast-granum-a-4, chloroplast-granum-b-4, chloroplast-lamella-4, chloroplast-granum-a-5, chloroplast-granum-b-5, chloroplast-lamella-5, chloroplast-granum-a-6, chloroplast-granum-b-6, chloroplast-lamella-6, chloroplast-granum-a-7, chloroplast-granum-b-7, chloroplast-lamella-7): A double-membrane plastid containing chlorophyll and stacked thylakoid membranes. Function: Captures light energy and converts it into chemical energy during photosynthesis, releasing oxygen from water.
    - Fact: Chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis using chlorophyll and internal thylakoid membrane stacks called grana. [OpenStax, §4.3, 'Chloroplasts' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-3-eukaryotic-cells)]
    - Fact: Chloroplasts have a double membrane and their own circular DNA. [Encyclopaedia Britannica, Introduction, 'Chloroplast' (https://www.britannica.com/science/chloroplast)]
  - **Mitochondrion** (high confidence; meshes: mitochondrion-0, mitochondrion-cristae-0, mitochondrion-1, mitochondrion-cristae-1, mitochondrion-2, mitochondrion-cristae-2, mitochondrion-3, mitochondrion-cristae-3, mitochondrion-4, mitochondrion-cristae-4): A double-membrane organelle whose inner membrane is folded into cristae. Function: Produces ATP through aerobic respiration and participates in other metabolic pathways.
    - Fact: Mitochondria produce ATP by aerobic respiration, and their inner membrane is folded into cristae. [OpenStax, §4.3, 'Mitochondria' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-3-eukaryotic-cells)]
    - Fact: Mitochondria contain their own DNA and ribosomes and can divide independently of the cell cycle. [Encyclopaedia Britannica, Introduction, 'Mitochondrion' (https://www.britannica.com/science/mitochondrion)]
  - **Golgi apparatus** (high confidence; meshes: golgi, golgi-vesicle): A stack of flattened membrane sacs that modifies and sorts proteins and lipids. Function: Receives cargo from the endoplasmic reticulum, modifies it, and packages it into vesicles for delivery.
    - Fact: The Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts, and packages proteins and lipids into vesicles. [OpenStax, §4.4, 'The Golgi Apparatus' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-4-the-endomembrane-system-and-proteins)]
    - Fact: Golgi cisternae are flattened membrane sacs, often drawn as a stack. [National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI Bookshelf), Chapter 13, 'Intracellular Vesicular Traffic' (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK21054/)]

### White blood cell (Homo sapiens)

- **Domain / Cell type**: animal · Neutrophil (segmented granulocyte)
- **Size & scale**: Roughly 9–15 µm diameter — Schematic and unitless. The pseudopods and granules are enlarged for legibility; no real-world scale is encoded.
- **3D stats**: 84 mesh instances · ~21,392 estimated triangles · Capabilities: 3D procedural mesh, Structure camera focus, Cutaway shell toggle, Mesh-mapped highlighting, PNG screenshot export, GLB export capability · Preview: `/previews/white-blood-cell.svg`
- **Summary**: A motile immune cell with a multi-lobed nucleus, enzyme-rich granules, and actin-driven pseudopods.
- **Overview**: Neutrophils patrol blood and tissue, following chemical cues to sites of infection. They are specialised for rapid response: a lobed nucleus, abundant granules, and a flexible actin cytoskeleton let them squeeze through tissue and engulf microbes. This schematic emphasises those features; granule counts and nuclear lobe shape vary between real cells.
- **Traits**: Nucleus: Present, multi-lobed | Cell wall: Absent | Chloroplasts: Absent | Motility: Amoeboid; chemotaxis | Typical size: 9–15 µm | Organisation: Eukaryotic, single cell in blood/tissue
- **Structures (6)**:
  - **Plasma membrane** (high confidence; meshes: plasma-membrane): The selectively permeable outer membrane of the neutrophil, specialised for sensing, adhesion, and engulfment. Function: Controls exchange, carries chemotactic receptors, and rearranges to form a phagosome around a target.
    - Fact: The neutrophil plasma membrane carries receptors that detect chemical signals and adhesion molecules used during migration. [Encyclopaedia Britannica, Introduction, 'Neutrophil' (https://www.britannica.com/science/neutrophil)]
    - Fact: During phagocytosis the plasma membrane extends around a particle and pinches off to form an internal vesicle. [OpenStax, §18.4, 'Leukocytes' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/18-4-leukocytes-and-platelets)]
  - **Multi-lobed nucleus** (high confidence; meshes: nucleus-lobe-0, nucleus-lobe-1, nucleus-lobe-2, nucleus-lobe-3, nucleus-bridge-0, nucleus-bridge-1, nucleus-bridge-2): A nucleus divided into several connected lobes, characteristic of mature segmented neutrophils. Function: Houses the cell's DNA; the lobed shape is associated with the mature, circulating form of the cell.
    - Fact: Mature neutrophils typically have a nucleus with three to five connected lobes. [OpenStax, §18.4, 'Leukocytes' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/18-4-leukocytes-and-platelets)]
    - Fact: Neutrophils are granulocytes: leukocytes characterised by prominent cytoplasmic granules and a lobed nucleus. [Encyclopaedia Britannica, Introduction, 'Neutrophil' (https://www.britannica.com/science/neutrophil)]
  - **Cytoplasmic granules** (high confidence; meshes: granules-primary, granules-secondary): Membrane-bound storage vesicles containing enzymes and antimicrobial compounds. Function: Release their contents into a phagosome or the extracellular space to kill and digest microbes.
    - Fact: Neutrophil granules store enzymes and antimicrobial proteins that are released during the immune response. [Encyclopaedia Britannica, Introduction, 'Neutrophil' (https://www.britannica.com/science/neutrophil)]
    - Fact: Granulocytes are named for their prominent cytoplasmic granules. [OpenStax, §18.4, 'Leukocytes' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/18-4-leukocytes-and-platelets)]
  - **Mitochondrion** (high confidence; meshes: mitochondrion-0, mitochondrion-cristae-0, mitochondrion-1, mitochondrion-cristae-1, mitochondrion-2, mitochondrion-cristae-2, mitochondrion-3, mitochondrion-cristae-3, mitochondrion-4, mitochondrion-cristae-4): A double-membrane organelle that generates ATP through aerobic metabolism. Function: Supplies energy for migration, granule release, and the respiratory burst used to kill microbes.
    - Fact: Mitochondria generate ATP by aerobic respiration and have an inner membrane folded into cristae. [Encyclopaedia Britannica, Introduction, 'Mitochondrion' (https://www.britannica.com/science/mitochondrion)]
    - Fact: Mitochondria contain their own DNA and ribosomes and can divide independently of the cell cycle. [Encyclopaedia Britannica, Introduction, 'Mitochondrion' (https://www.britannica.com/science/mitochondrion)]
  - **Pseudopod** (high confidence; meshes: pseudopod-0, pseudopod-1, pseudopod-2, pseudopod-3): A temporary cytoplasmic extension produced by actin polymerisation at the leading edge. Function: Drives amoeboid crawling toward chemical signals and reaches around particles during phagocytosis.
    - Fact: Neutrophils move through tissue and engulf microbes by extending actin-rich pseudopods. [Encyclopaedia Britannica, Introduction, 'Neutrophil' (https://www.britannica.com/science/neutrophil)]
    - Fact: Amoeboid movement depends on the polymerisation and depolymerisation of actin filaments. [National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI Bookshelf), Chapter 16, 'The Cytoskeleton' (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK21054/)]
  - **Actin cytoskeleton** (high confidence; meshes: actin-filament-0, actin-filament-1, actin-filament-2, actin-filament-3, actin-filament-4, actin-filament-5, actin-filament-6, actin-filament-7, actin-filament-8, actin-filament-9): A dynamic network of actin filaments that supports shape change and force generation. Function: Powers crawling, membrane ruffling, and the contractile ring used to internalise a phagosome.
    - Fact: Actin filaments are polar polymers that assemble and disassemble to drive cell shape change and movement. [National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI Bookshelf), Chapter 16, 'The Cytoskeleton' (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK21054/)]
    - Fact: Phagocytosis requires coordinated actin polymerisation beneath the plasma membrane. [Encyclopaedia Britannica, Introduction, 'Neutrophil' (https://www.britannica.com/science/neutrophil)]

### Neuron (Mammalian (schematic))

- **Domain / Cell type**: animal · Multipolar motor neuron
- **Size & scale**: Soma 10–30 µm; axon may extend up to about a metre in humans — Schematic and unitless. Axon length is compressed; the model cannot be used to estimate real dimensions.
- **3D stats**: 85 mesh instances · ~25,476 estimated triangles · Capabilities: 3D procedural mesh, Structure camera focus, Cutaway shell toggle, Mesh-mapped highlighting, PNG screenshot export, GLB export capability · Preview: `/previews/neuron.svg`
- **Summary**: A signal-conducting cell with a receptive soma and dendrites, a long axon, insulating myelin, and transmitter-releasing terminals.
- **Overview**: Neurons are polarised cells built for communication. Dendrites collect inputs, the soma integrates them, and the axon carries an action potential to terminals that release neurotransmitter onto the next cell. The myelin sheath shown here is a schematic of the insulating wrapping provided by glial cells. Real neurons vary enormously in shape, and many have thousands of synaptic contacts not depicted here.
- **Traits**: Nucleus: Present | Cell wall: Absent | Chloroplasts: Absent | Motility: No crawling; conducts electrical signals | Typical size: Soma 10–30 µm; axon up to ~1 m | Organisation: Eukaryotic, nervous tissue
- **Structures (7)**:
  - **Soma (cell body)** (high confidence; meshes: soma, axon-hillock, soma-nissl-0, soma-nissl-1, soma-nissl-2): The compact cell body containing the nucleus and most biosynthetic machinery. Function: Integrates incoming signals and maintains the cell's metabolism; it is the origin of the axon.
    - Fact: The neuronal cell body, or soma, contains the nucleus and most of the cell's organelles. [OpenStax, §35.1, 'Neurons' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/35-1-neurons-and-glial-cells)]
    - Fact: In a multipolar neuron, dendrites and a single axon extend from the cell body. [OpenStax, §35.1, 'Neurons' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/35-1-neurons-and-glial-cells)]
  - **Nucleus** (high confidence; meshes: nucleus, nucleus-chromatin, nucleolus, nuclear-pore): The neuron's DNA-containing organelle, with a prominent nucleolus in many active neurons. Function: Directs protein synthesis needed for neurotransmission, plasticity, and cell maintenance.
    - Fact: The neuronal nucleus contains the cell's genetic material and is typically centred in the soma. [OpenStax, §35.1, 'Neurons' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/35-1-neurons-and-glial-cells)]
    - Fact: A prominent nucleolus is a common feature of metabolically active neurons. [National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI Bookshelf), Chapter 12, 'Intracellular Compartments and Protein Sorting' (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK21054/)]
  - **Dendrites** (high confidence; meshes: dendrite-trunk-0, dendrite-trunk-1, dendrite-trunk-2, dendrite-trunk-3, dendrite-trunk-4, dendrite-trunk-5, dendrite-branch-0, dendrite-spine-0, dendrite-branch-1, dendrite-spine-1, dendrite-branch-2, dendrite-spine-2, dendrite-branch-3, dendrite-spine-3, dendrite-branch-4, dendrite-spine-4, dendrite-branch-5, dendrite-spine-5, dendrite-branch-6, dendrite-spine-6, dendrite-branch-7, dendrite-spine-7, dendrite-branch-8, dendrite-spine-8, dendrite-branch-9, dendrite-spine-9): Branching processes that receive synaptic inputs and carry graded signals toward the soma. Function: Increase the receptive surface area and integrate inputs from other neurons.
    - Fact: Dendrites are branched processes that receive signals and conduct graded potentials toward the cell body. [OpenStax, §35.1, 'Neurons' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/35-1-neurons-and-glial-cells)]
    - Fact: Dendritic branching greatly expands the surface available for synaptic contacts. [OpenStax, §35.2, 'How Neurons Communicate' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/35-2-how-neurons-communicate)]
  - **Axon** (high confidence; meshes: axon, axon-node-0, axon-node-1, axon-node-2, axon-node-3): A single long process that conducts action potentials away from the soma toward axon terminals. Function: Transmits electrical signals over distance without decrement, thanks to voltage-gated ion channels.
    - Fact: The axon carries action potentials away from the cell body toward its terminals. [OpenStax, §35.1, 'Neurons' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/35-1-neurons-and-glial-cells)]
    - Fact: Action potentials are regenerated along the axon by voltage-gated ion channels rather than decaying with distance. [OpenStax, §35.2, 'How Neurons Communicate' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/35-2-how-neurons-communicate)]
  - **Myelin sheath** (high confidence; meshes: myelin-sheath-0, myelin-core-0, myelin-sheath-1, myelin-core-1, myelin-sheath-2, myelin-core-2, myelin-sheath-3, myelin-core-3, myelin-sheath-4, myelin-core-4): A multilayered glial wrapping around segments of some axons, interrupted at nodes of Ranvier. Function: Electrically insulates the axon and enables fast saltatory conduction between nodes.
    - Fact: In the peripheral nervous system myelin is produced by Schwann cells; in the central nervous system by oligodendrocytes. [OpenStax, §35.1, 'Glial Cells' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/35-1-neurons-and-glial-cells)]
    - Fact: Myelination increases conduction velocity by allowing the action potential to jump between nodes of Ranvier. [OpenStax, §35.2, 'How Neurons Communicate' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/35-2-how-neurons-communicate)]
  - **Axon terminals** (high confidence; meshes: axon-branch-0, axon-bouton-0, axon-vesicle-a-0, axon-vesicle-b-0, axon-branch-1, axon-bouton-1, axon-vesicle-a-1, axon-vesicle-b-1, axon-branch-2, axon-bouton-2, axon-vesicle-a-2, axon-vesicle-b-2, axon-branch-3, axon-bouton-3, axon-vesicle-a-3, axon-vesicle-b-3): Specialised endings where the axon contacts a target cell and releases neurotransmitter. Function: Convert an incoming action potential into chemical signalling across a synapse.
    - Fact: Axon terminals contain synaptic vesicles that release neurotransmitter when calcium enters after an action potential. [OpenStax, §35.2, 'How Neurons Communicate' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/35-2-how-neurons-communicate)]
    - Fact: A synapse is the junction where a presynaptic terminal communicates with a postsynaptic cell. [OpenStax, §35.2, 'How Neurons Communicate' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/35-2-how-neurons-communicate)]
  - **Mitochondrion** (high confidence; meshes: mitochondrion-0, mitochondrion-cristae-0, mitochondrion-1, mitochondrion-cristae-1, mitochondrion-2, mitochondrion-cristae-2, mitochondrion-3, mitochondrion-cristae-3, mitochondrion-4, mitochondrion-cristae-4): An ATP-generating organelle enriched in regions with high energy demand such as terminals. Function: Supplies ATP for ion pumps, vesicle trafficking, and neurotransmitter recycling.
    - Fact: Mitochondria generate ATP by aerobic respiration and are distributed to regions of high energy demand in neurons. [Encyclopaedia Britannica, Introduction, 'Mitochondrion' (https://www.britannica.com/science/mitochondrion)]
    - Fact: Restoring ion gradients after action potentials requires ATP-driven pumps. [OpenStax, §35.2, 'How Neurons Communicate' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/35-2-how-neurons-communicate)]

### Epithelial cell (Homo sapiens)

- **Domain / Cell type**: animal · Intestinal enterocyte
- **Size & scale**: Roughly 10 µm wide and 20 µm tall — Schematic and unitless. Microvillus density and membrane thickness are exaggerated for legibility.
- **3D stats**: 137 mesh instances · ~38,256 estimated triangles · Capabilities: 3D procedural mesh, Structure camera focus, Cutaway shell toggle, Mesh-mapped highlighting, PNG screenshot export, GLB export capability · Preview: `/previews/epithelial-cell.svg`
- **Summary**: A polarised absorptive cell: a dense apical brush border, a sealing tight junction, and energy-hungry basolateral transport.
- **Overview**: Enterocytes line the small intestine and absorb nutrients. Their apical surface carries a dense brush border of microvilli, while their basolateral surface contacts neighbouring cells and the basement membrane. Tight junctions separate these domains and limit leakage between cells. This schematic highlights that polarity rather than the full cytoskeletal and membrane architecture.
- **Traits**: Nucleus: Present | Cell wall: Absent | Chloroplasts: Absent | Motility: Anchored; polarised sheet | Typical size: ~10 µm wide, 20 µm tall | Organisation: Eukaryotic, epithelial sheet
- **Structures (7)**:
  - **Apical brush border** (high confidence; meshes: apical-membrane, microvillus): A dense array of actin-supported microvilli on the apical membrane, forming the brush border. Function: Multiplies the apical surface area for nutrient and ion absorption.
    - Fact: Microvilli are narrow membrane projections that increase a cell's apical surface area; in the intestine they form the brush border. [OpenStax, §4.2, 'Epithelial Tissue' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/4-2-epithelial-tissue)]
    - Fact: Each microvillus contains a core of actin filaments that supports its shape. [National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI Bookshelf), Chapter 16, 'The Cytoskeleton' (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK21054/)]
  - **Tight junction** (high confidence; meshes: tight-junction, tight-junction-lower): A belt-like junction near the apical surface that seals the space between adjacent epithelial cells. Function: Limits paracellular leakage and helps separate apical from basolateral membrane domains.
    - Fact: Tight junctions form a seal between adjacent epithelial cells that limits movement of material through the paracellular space. [OpenStax, §4.6, 'Tight Junctions' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-6-connections-between-cells-and-cellular-activities)]
    - Fact: Tight junctions help maintain the separate apical and basolateral domains of epithelial cells. [OpenStax, §4.2, 'Epithelial Tissue' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/4-2-epithelial-tissue)]
  - **Basolateral membrane** (high confidence; meshes: basolateral-shell, basolateral-contact, desmosome-0, desmosome-1, desmosome-2, desmosome-3, desmosome-4, desmosome-5): The side and basal surfaces of the cell that contact neighbouring cells and the basement membrane. Function: Carries transporters that move absorbed nutrients into the blood and maintain ion gradients.
    - Fact: Epithelial cells are polarised, with distinct apical and basolateral membrane domains carrying different transport proteins. [OpenStax, §4.2, 'Epithelial Tissue' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/4-2-epithelial-tissue)]
    - Fact: The basolateral surface rests on a basement membrane and faces the underlying connective tissue. [OpenStax, §4.2, 'Epithelial Tissue' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/4-2-epithelial-tissue)]
  - **Nucleus** (high confidence; meshes: nucleus, nucleus-chromatin, nucleolus, nuclear-pore): The DNA-containing organelle, positioned toward the basal side of this polarised cell. Function: Controls protein synthesis, including the transporters and enzymes needed for absorption.
    - Fact: The nucleus contains the cell's chromosomal DNA and directs protein synthesis. [OpenStax, §4.3, 'The Nucleus' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-3-eukaryotic-cells)]
    - Fact: In columnar epithelial cells the nucleus is often located toward the basal region. [OpenStax, §4.2, 'Epithelial Tissue' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/4-2-epithelial-tissue)]
  - **Mitochondrion** (high confidence; meshes: mitochondrion-0, mitochondrion-cristae-0, mitochondrion-1, mitochondrion-cristae-1, mitochondrion-2, mitochondrion-cristae-2, mitochondrion-3, mitochondrion-cristae-3, mitochondrion-4, mitochondrion-cristae-4, mitochondrion-5, mitochondrion-cristae-5): An ATP-producing organelle abundant in absorptive epithelial cells. Function: Powers active transport across the apical and basolateral membranes.
    - Fact: Mitochondria produce ATP by aerobic respiration, and their inner membrane is folded into cristae. [OpenStax, §4.3, 'Mitochondria' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-3-eukaryotic-cells)]
    - Fact: Nutrient absorption depends on active transport, which requires a continuous supply of ATP. [OpenStax, §4.2, 'Epithelial Tissue' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/4-2-epithelial-tissue)]
  - **Rough endoplasmic reticulum** (high confidence; meshes: rough-er-sheet, rough-er-ribosome): A network of ribosome-studded membrane sheets specialised for protein synthesis. Function: Produces membrane proteins, secreted enzymes, and transporters for the cell's absorptive role.
    - Fact: Rough endoplasmic reticulum is studded with ribosomes and is a major site of protein synthesis. [OpenStax, §4.4, 'The Endoplasmic Reticulum' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-4-the-endomembrane-system-and-proteins)]
    - Fact: Proteins synthesised in the rough ER are folded and modified before moving to the Golgi. [OpenStax, §4.4, 'The Endoplasmic Reticulum' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-4-the-endomembrane-system-and-proteins)]
  - **Golgi apparatus** (high confidence; meshes: golgi, golgi-vesicle): A stack of flattened membrane sacs that modifies, sorts, and packages proteins. Function: Routes newly made membrane and secreted proteins to their correct destinations.
    - Fact: The Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts, and packages proteins and lipids into vesicles. [OpenStax, §4.4, 'The Golgi Apparatus' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-4-the-endomembrane-system-and-proteins)]
    - Fact: The Golgi is part of the endomembrane system and receives cargo from the endoplasmic reticulum. [OpenStax, §4.4, 'The Endomembrane System' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-4-the-endomembrane-system-and-proteins)]

### Bacterium (Escherichia coli)

- **Domain / Cell type**: bacteria · Gram-negative rod
- **Size & scale**: Roughly 0.5 µm wide and 2 µm long — Schematic and unitless. Ribosome number, pili density, and flagellar length are approximate teaching choices.
- **3D stats**: 93 mesh instances · ~43,656 estimated triangles · Capabilities: 3D procedural mesh, Structure camera focus, Cutaway shell toggle, Mesh-mapped highlighting, PNG screenshot export, GLB export capability · Preview: `/previews/bacteria.svg`
- **Summary**: A prokaryotic cell: no membrane-bound nucleus, a layered envelope, a nucleoid, 70S ribosomes, and a rotary flagellum.
- **Overview**: Bacteria are prokaryotes: their DNA is not enclosed in a membrane-bound nucleus, and they lack the membrane-bound organelles of eukaryotes. This schematic E. coli shows the Gram-negative envelope (outer membrane, peptidoglycan wall, inner membrane), a tangled nucleoid, ribosomes, a helical flagellum, and surface pili. The envelope cutaway is authored so the interior can be inspected without pretending to be a physical slice.
- **Traits**: Nucleus: Absent (nucleoid instead) | Cell wall: Peptidoglycan envelope | Chloroplasts: Absent | Motility: Flagellar swimming | Typical size: ~0.5 × 2 µm | Organisation: Prokaryotic, single cell
- **Structures (7)**:
  - **Outer membrane** (high confidence; meshes: outer-membrane, outer-porin-0, outer-porin-1, outer-porin-2, outer-porin-3, outer-porin-4): The outermost lipid bilayer of the Gram-negative cell envelope, outside the peptidoglycan layer. Function: Forms a permeability barrier and contains proteins that mediate transport and structural connections.
    - Fact: Gram-negative bacteria have an outer membrane outside a thin peptidoglycan layer, with an inner membrane beneath it. [OpenStax, §4.2, 'Prokaryotic Cells' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-2-prokaryotic-cells)]
    - Fact: The outer membrane is a lipid bilayer containing proteins that control passage of many substances. [National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI Bookshelf), Chapter 1, 'Cells and Genomes' (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK21054/)]
  - **Peptidoglycan cell wall** (high confidence; meshes: cell-wall): A mesh polymer of sugars and short peptides that lies between the two membranes of a Gram-negative rod. Function: Maintains cell shape and resists osmotic pressure; its synthesis is the target of penicillin-type antibiotics.
    - Fact: The bacterial cell wall contains peptidoglycan, a polymer that helps maintain cell shape and withstand osmotic pressure. [OpenStax, §4.2, 'Prokaryotic Cells' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-2-prokaryotic-cells)]
    - Fact: Gram-negative bacteria have a comparatively thin peptidoglycan layer between their inner and outer membranes. [OpenStax, §4.2, 'Prokaryotic Cells' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-2-prokaryotic-cells)]
  - **Plasma membrane** (high confidence; meshes: plasma-membrane): The inner lipid bilayer that encloses the bacterial cytoplasm. Function: Regulates transport and hosts many energy-conversion and biosynthetic systems.
    - Fact: The bacterial plasma membrane is a phospholipid bilayer that regulates what enters and leaves the cell. [OpenStax, §4.2, 'Prokaryotic Cells' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-2-prokaryotic-cells)]
    - Fact: Because prokaryotes lack membrane-bound organelles, many membrane-associated functions occur at the plasma membrane. [OpenStax, §4.2, 'Prokaryotic Cells' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-2-prokaryotic-cells)]
  - **Nucleoid** (high confidence; meshes: nucleoid, nucleoid-loop-b, nucleoid-plasmid-a, nucleoid-plasmid-b): The region containing the bacterium's circular chromosome, not enclosed by a membrane. Function: Stores and replicates the genetic material; gene expression is coupled to transcription and translation.
    - Fact: Prokaryotic DNA is found in a nucleoid region that is not surrounded by a membrane. [OpenStax, §4.2, 'Prokaryotic Cells' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-2-prokaryotic-cells)]
    - Fact: The E. coli chromosome is a single circular DNA molecule. [National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI Bookshelf), Chapter 1, 'Cells and Genomes' (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK21054/)]
  - **Ribosome** (high confidence; meshes: ribosome): A ribonucleoprotein machine that translates messenger RNA into protein. Function: Synthesises proteins, using a 70S bacterial ribosome rather than the 80S eukaryotic type.
    - Fact: Bacterial ribosomes are 70S particles, distinct from the 80S ribosomes of eukaryotic cytoplasm. [OpenStax, §4.2, 'Prokaryotic Cells' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-2-prokaryotic-cells)]
    - Fact: Ribosomes translate mRNA into protein and are found throughout the bacterial cytoplasm. [OpenStax, §4.2, 'Prokaryotic Cells' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-2-prokaryotic-cells)]
  - **Flagellum** (high confidence; meshes: flagellum-filament, flagellum-filament-b, flagellum-hook, flagellum-motor-l, flagellum-motor-ms): A long helical filament rotated by a membrane-embedded motor to propel the cell. Function: Drives swimming motility and chemotaxis toward favourable conditions.
    - Fact: A bacterial flagellum is a helical filament rotated by a molecular motor anchored in the cell envelope. [Encyclopaedia Britannica, Introduction, 'Flagellum' (https://www.britannica.com/science/flagellum)]
    - Fact: Bacterial flagella rotate to push or pull the cell through liquid. [OpenStax, §4.2, 'Prokaryotic Cells' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-2-prokaryotic-cells)]
  - **Pili** (high confidence; meshes: pilus-0, pilus-1, pilus-2, pilus-3, pilus-4, pilus-5, pilus-6, pilus-7, pilus-8, pilus-9, pilus-10, pilus-11, pilus-12, pilus-13, pilus-14, pilus-15, pilus-16, pilus-17, pilus-18, pilus-19, pilus-20, pilus-21, pilus-22, pilus-23): Short protein appendages on the bacterial surface, distinct from the flagellum. Function: Mediate attachment to surfaces and, for some pili, horizontal DNA transfer between cells.
    - Fact: Pili are short appendages that help bacteria attach to surfaces and to other cells. [OpenStax, §4.2, 'Prokaryotic Cells' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-2-prokaryotic-cells)]
    - Fact: Specialised pili can mediate conjugation, the transfer of DNA between bacterial cells. [National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI Bookshelf), Chapter 1, 'Cells and Genomes' (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK21054/)]

### Animal cell (Mammalia (unspecified lineage))

- **Domain / Cell type**: animal · Generic mammalian cell
- **Size & scale**: Commonly 10–30 µm across — Schematic and unitless. Organelle size, number, and position vary by cell type and are not measured.
- **3D stats**: 115 mesh instances · ~26,396 estimated triangles · Capabilities: 3D procedural mesh, Structure camera focus, Cutaway shell toggle, Mesh-mapped highlighting, PNG screenshot export, GLB export capability · Preview: `/previews/animal-cell.svg`
- **Summary**: A generalised eukaryotic animal cell: no wall or chloroplasts, but a nucleus, endomembrane system, mitochondria, and lysosomes.
- **Overview**: This specimen is a reference animal cell rather than a portrait of one particular cell type. It shows features shared by most mammalian cells: a flexible plasma membrane, a nucleus, rough and smooth endoplasmic reticulum, a Golgi apparatus, mitochondria, and lysosomes. Specialised cells add their own structures—muscle sarcomeres, neuronal processes, epithelial junctions—which are represented by the other specimens.
- **Traits**: Nucleus: Present | Cell wall: Absent | Chloroplasts: Absent | Motility: Limited; lineage-dependent | Typical size: 10–30 µm | Organisation: Eukaryotic, animal tissue
- **Structures (7)**:
  - **Plasma membrane** (high confidence; meshes: plasma-membrane): The flexible outer phospholipid bilayer that defines the cell and mediates exchange. Function: Controls transport, receives signals, and anchors the cell to neighbours and the extracellular matrix.
    - Fact: The plasma membrane is a phospholipid bilayer with embedded proteins that regulates transport and signalling. [OpenStax, §4.3, 'The Plasma Membrane' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-3-eukaryotic-cells)]
    - Fact: Animal cells lack a cell wall; their shape is supported by the cytoskeleton and extracellular matrix. [OpenStax, §4.5, 'The Cytoskeleton' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-5-the-cytoskeleton)]
  - **Nucleus** (high confidence; meshes: nucleus, nucleus-chromatin, nucleolus, nuclear-pore): The double-membrane organelle that houses the cell's chromosomal DNA. Function: Stores genetic information and coordinates transcription, growth, and division.
    - Fact: The nucleus is bounded by a nuclear envelope with pores and contains the cell's chromosomal DNA. [OpenStax, §4.3, 'The Nucleus' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-3-eukaryotic-cells)]
    - Fact: The nucleolus assembles ribosomal subunits. [OpenStax, §4.3, 'The Nucleus' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-3-eukaryotic-cells)]
  - **Rough endoplasmic reticulum** (high confidence; meshes: rough-er-0, rough-er-1, rough-er-2, rough-er-3, rough-er-4, rough-er-5, rough-er-ribosome): Flattened membrane cisternae studded with ribosomes, continuous with the nuclear envelope. Function: Synthesises and folds membrane and secreted proteins, then routes them toward the Golgi.
    - Fact: Rough endoplasmic reticulum is studded with ribosomes and is a major site of protein synthesis. [OpenStax, §4.4, 'The Endoplasmic Reticulum' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-4-the-endomembrane-system-and-proteins)]
    - Fact: The rough ER is continuous with the outer nuclear membrane and passes proteins to the Golgi. [OpenStax, §4.4, 'The Endoplasmic Reticulum' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-4-the-endomembrane-system-and-proteins)]
  - **Smooth endoplasmic reticulum** (high confidence; meshes: smooth-er-0, smooth-er-1, smooth-er-2, smooth-er-3, smooth-er-4, smooth-er-5, smooth-er-6, smooth-er-7, smooth-er-8): A tubular ER network lacking ribosomes, specialised for lipid and steroid synthesis and detoxification. Function: Produces lipids, stores calcium, and helps metabolise drugs and toxins in some cell types.
    - Fact: Smooth ER lacks ribosomes and is associated with lipid synthesis, detoxification, and calcium storage. [OpenStax, §4.4, 'The Endoplasmic Reticulum' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-4-the-endomembrane-system-and-proteins)]
    - Fact: The amount of smooth ER varies greatly with cell function. [National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI Bookshelf), Chapter 12, 'Intracellular Compartments and Protein Sorting' (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK21054/)]
  - **Golgi apparatus** (high confidence; meshes: golgi, golgi-vesicle): A stack of flattened membrane cisternae that modifies and sorts proteins and lipids. Function: Receives cargo from the ER, modifies it, and packages it into vesicles for delivery or secretion.
    - Fact: The Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts, and packages proteins and lipids into vesicles. [OpenStax, §4.4, 'The Golgi Apparatus' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-4-the-endomembrane-system-and-proteins)]
    - Fact: Golgi cisternae are flattened membrane sacs with distinct entry and exit faces. [National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI Bookshelf), Chapter 13, 'Intracellular Vesicular Traffic' (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK21054/)]
  - **Mitochondrion** (high confidence; meshes: mitochondrion-0, mitochondrion-cristae-0, mitochondrion-1, mitochondrion-cristae-1, mitochondrion-2, mitochondrion-cristae-2, mitochondrion-3, mitochondrion-cristae-3, mitochondrion-4, mitochondrion-cristae-4, mitochondrion-5, mitochondrion-cristae-5): A double-membrane organelle with cristae that produces ATP by aerobic respiration. Function: Supplies most of the cell's ATP and participates in calcium and metabolic signalling.
    - Fact: Mitochondria produce ATP by aerobic respiration, and their inner membrane is folded into cristae. [OpenStax, §4.3, 'Mitochondria' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-3-eukaryotic-cells)]
    - Fact: Mitochondria contain their own DNA and ribosomes. [Encyclopaedia Britannica, Introduction, 'Mitochondrion' (https://www.britannica.com/science/mitochondrion)]
  - **Lysosome** (high confidence; meshes: lysosome-0, lysosome-core-0, lysosome-1, lysosome-core-1, lysosome-2, lysosome-core-2, lysosome-3, lysosome-core-3, lysosome-4, lysosome-core-4, lysosome-5, lysosome-core-5, lysosome-6, lysosome-core-6): An acidic, membrane-bound organelle containing hydrolytic enzymes. Function: Digests material taken in by endocytosis and recycles damaged cell components through autophagy.
    - Fact: Lysosomes contain hydrolytic enzymes that function at acidic pH and digest engulfed material or worn-out organelles. [OpenStax, §4.3, 'Lysosomes' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-3-eukaryotic-cells)]
    - Fact: Lysosomal membranes keep digestive enzymes separated from the cytosol. [National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI Bookshelf), Chapter 13, 'Intracellular Vesicular Traffic' (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK21054/)]

### Muscle cell (Homo sapiens)

- **Domain / Cell type**: animal · Skeletal muscle fiber
- **Size & scale**: Diameter roughly 10–100 µm; length up to several centimetres — Schematic and unitless. Sarcomere spacing is widened for visibility; the model cannot be measured for real dimensions.
- **3D stats**: 81 mesh instances · ~24,736 estimated triangles · Capabilities: 3D procedural mesh, Structure camera focus, Cutaway shell toggle, Mesh-mapped highlighting, PNG screenshot export, GLB export capability · Preview: `/previews/muscle-cell.svg`
- **Summary**: A contractile syncytium: bundled myofibrils, repeating sarcomeres, T-tubules, calcium-storing sarcoplasmic reticulum, and peripheral nuclei.
- **Overview**: Skeletal muscle fibres are built for force. Each fibre contains bundles of myofibrils, and each myofibril is a chain of sarcomeres—the repeating units where actin and myosin filaments slide past one another. Excitation spreads deep into the fibre along T-tubules and triggers calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. This schematic shows the architecture, not the molecular filament arrangement, and is not to scale along the fibre.
- **Traits**: Nucleus: Present; multiple, peripheral | Cell wall: Absent | Chloroplasts: Absent | Motility: Contractile (sarcomere shortening) | Typical size: 10–100 µm diameter; up to cm long | Organisation: Eukaryotic, multinucleated syncytium
- **Structures (7)**:
  - **Sarcolemma** (high confidence; meshes: sarcolemma): The plasma membrane of a muscle fiber, capable of conducting an action potential. Function: Receives motor-neuron signals and propagates excitation along and into the fibre.
    - Fact: The sarcolemma is the plasma membrane of a muscle fiber and is excitable like other muscle membranes. [OpenStax, §10.2, 'Muscle Fiber Contraction and Relaxation' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/10-2-muscle-fiber-contraction-and-relaxation)]
    - Fact: The sarcolemma invaginates to form T-tubules that carry excitation deep into the fiber. [OpenStax, §10.2, 'Muscle Fiber Contraction and Relaxation' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/10-2-muscle-fiber-contraction-and-relaxation)]
  - **Myofibril** (high confidence; meshes: myofibril-center, myofibril-inner, myofibril): A long bundle of actin and myosin filaments running the length of the muscle fiber. Function: Generates force through the coordinated shortening of its sarcomeres.
    - Fact: A muscle fiber contains many myofibrils, each made of repeating contractile units called sarcomeres. [OpenStax, §10.2, 'Muscle Fiber Contraction and Relaxation' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/10-2-muscle-fiber-contraction-and-relaxation)]
    - Fact: The regular arrangement of myofilaments gives skeletal muscle its striated appearance. [OpenStax, §10.1, 'Overview of Muscle Tissues' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/10-1-overview-of-muscle-tissues)]
  - **Sarcomere** (high confidence; meshes: sarcomere-z-0, sarcomere-z-1, sarcomere-z-2, sarcomere-z-3, sarcomere-z-4, sarcomere-z-5, sarcomere-z-6, sarcomere-a-0, sarcomere-a-1, sarcomere-a-2, sarcomere-a-3, sarcomere-a-4, sarcomere-a-5): The repeating contractile unit between adjacent Z discs, containing actin and myosin filaments. Function: Shortens when myosin heads cycle along actin, pulling Z discs closer together.
    - Fact: A sarcomere is the basic contractile unit of striated muscle, bounded by Z discs. [Encyclopaedia Britannica, Introduction, 'Sarcomere' (https://www.britannica.com/science/sarcomere)]
    - Fact: During contraction, actin and myosin filaments slide past each other and the sarcomere shortens. [OpenStax, §10.2, 'Muscle Fiber Contraction and Relaxation' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/10-2-muscle-fiber-contraction-and-relaxation)]
  - **T-tubule** (high confidence; meshes: t-tubule-ring-0, t-tubule-cross-0, t-tubule-ring-1, t-tubule-cross-1, t-tubule-ring-2, t-tubule-cross-2, t-tubule-ring-3, t-tubule-cross-3): An invagination of the sarcolemma that carries excitation deep into the muscle fiber. Function: Brings the action potential close to the sarcoplasmic reticulum so calcium release is synchronised.
    - Fact: T-tubules are inward extensions of the sarcolemma that conduct action potentials deep into the fiber. [OpenStax, §10.2, 'Muscle Fiber Contraction and Relaxation' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/10-2-muscle-fiber-contraction-and-relaxation)]
    - Fact: A T-tubule together with flanking terminal cisternae of the sarcoplasmic reticulum forms a triad. [OpenStax, §10.2, 'Muscle Fiber Contraction and Relaxation' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/10-2-muscle-fiber-contraction-and-relaxation)]
  - **Sarcoplasmic reticulum** (high confidence; meshes: sr-cisterna-l-0, sr-cisterna-r-0, sr-cisterna-l-1, sr-cisterna-r-1, sr-cisterna-l-2, sr-cisterna-r-2, sr-cisterna-l-3, sr-cisterna-r-3, sarcoplasmic-reticulum): A specialised endoplasmic reticulum that stores and releases calcium ions. Function: Releases Ca²⁺ to trigger contraction and pumps it back to allow relaxation.
    - Fact: The sarcoplasmic reticulum stores calcium and releases it when an action potential reaches the T-tubule system. [OpenStax, §10.2, 'Muscle Fiber Contraction and Relaxation' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/10-2-muscle-fiber-contraction-and-relaxation)]
    - Fact: Calcium reuptake into the sarcoplasmic reticulum is required for muscle relaxation. [OpenStax, §10.2, 'Muscle Fiber Contraction and Relaxation' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/10-2-muscle-fiber-contraction-and-relaxation)]
  - **Mitochondrion** (high confidence; meshes: mitochondrion-0, mitochondrion-cristae-0, mitochondrion-1, mitochondrion-cristae-1, mitochondrion-2, mitochondrion-cristae-2, mitochondrion-3, mitochondrion-cristae-3, mitochondrion-4, mitochondrion-cristae-4, mitochondrion-5, mitochondrion-cristae-5, mitochondrion-6, mitochondrion-cristae-6, mitochondrion-7, mitochondrion-cristae-7): An ATP-producing organelle packed between myofibrils in active muscle fibers. Function: Supplies ATP for contraction and for the calcium and ion pumps that restore the resting state.
    - Fact: Muscle fibers are rich in mitochondria because contraction and ion pumping consume large amounts of ATP. [OpenStax, §10.2, 'Muscle Fiber Contraction and Relaxation' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/10-2-muscle-fiber-contraction-and-relaxation)]
    - Fact: Mitochondria produce ATP by aerobic respiration. [Encyclopaedia Britannica, Introduction, 'Mitochondrion' (https://www.britannica.com/science/mitochondrion)]
  - **Nucleus** (high confidence; meshes: nucleus-peripheral-0, nucleolus-peripheral-0, nucleus-peripheral-1, nucleolus-peripheral-1, nucleus-peripheral-2, nucleolus-peripheral-2, nucleus-peripheral-3, nucleolus-peripheral-3): One of many nuclei located at the periphery of a skeletal muscle fiber. Function: Directs protein synthesis for the large cytoplasmic volume of the fibre.
    - Fact: Skeletal muscle fibers are multinucleated, and their nuclei are typically located at the periphery. [OpenStax, §10.1, 'Overview of Muscle Tissues' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/10-1-overview-of-muscle-tissues)]
    - Fact: Multiple nuclei support protein synthesis across the large volume of a muscle fiber. [OpenStax, §10.2, 'Muscle Fiber Contraction and Relaxation' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/10-2-muscle-fiber-contraction-and-relaxation)]

### Red blood cell (Homo sapiens)

- **Domain / Cell type**: animal · Mature mammalian erythrocyte
- **Size & scale**: Roughly 7–8 µm diameter, ~2.5 µm thick at the rim — Schematic and unitless. Protein complexes and sugar chains are vastly enlarged relative to the cell disc so their spatial roles can be explored.
- **3D stats**: 140 mesh instances · ~21,592 estimated triangles · Capabilities: 3D procedural mesh, Structure camera focus, Cutaway shell toggle, Mesh-mapped highlighting, PNG screenshot export, GLB export capability · Preview: `/previews/red-blood-cell.svg`
- **Summary**: A flexible, anucleate biconcave disc packed with hemoglobin and supported by a sub-membrane spectrin skeleton for gas transport.
- **Overview**: Red blood cells are stripped down for oxygen and carbon dioxide transport. Lacking a nucleus and mitochondria leaves maximum space for hemoglobin while a biconcave geometry speeds gas diffusion and gives the cell deformability to squeeze through narrow capillaries. This schematic shows the membrane, underlying spectrin meshwork, hemoglobin matrix, ion exchangers, carbonic anhydrase, and surface glycocalyx at illustrative scales.
- **Traits**: Nucleus: Absent (enucleated when mature) | Cell wall: Absent | Chloroplasts: Absent | Motility: Passive (carried in blood flow) | Typical size: 7–8 µm | Organisation: Eukaryotic, specialised anucleate blood cell
- **Structures (6)**:
  - **Plasma membrane** (high confidence; meshes: plasma-membrane): A flexible, biconcave phospholipid bilayer encapsulating the erythrocyte cytoplasm without rigid walls. Function: Maximises surface-area-to-volume ratio for gas diffusion and resists shear stress as the cell bends through capillaries.
    - Fact: Human erythrocytes are biconcave discs that increase surface area for gas exchange and aid deformation through narrow capillaries. [OpenStax, §18.3, 'Erythrocytes' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/18-3-erythrocytes)]
    - Fact: The erythrocyte lipid bilayer is anchored from below by membrane-associated structural proteins to maintain integrity under blood-flow shear. [Encyclopaedia Britannica, Introduction, 'Red blood cell' (https://www.britannica.com/science/red-blood-cell)]
  - **Spectrin membrane skeleton** (high confidence; meshes: spectrin-strut-0, spectrin-strut-1, spectrin-strut-2, spectrin-strut-3, spectrin-strut-4, spectrin-strut-5, spectrin-strut-6, spectrin-strut-7, spectrin-strut-8, spectrin-strut-9, spectrin-strut-10, spectrin-strut-11, spectrin-strut-12, spectrin-strut-13, spectrin-strut-14, spectrin-strut-15, spectrin-strut-16, spectrin-strut-17, spectrin-strut-18, spectrin-strut-19, spectrin-strut-20, spectrin-strut-21, spectrin-strut-22, spectrin-strut-23, spectrin-strut-24, spectrin-strut-25, spectrin-strut-26, spectrin-strut-27, spectrin-strut-28, spectrin-strut-29, spectrin-strut-30, spectrin-strut-31, spectrin-strut-32, spectrin-strut-33, spectrin-strut-34, spectrin-strut-35, spectrin-strut-36, spectrin-strut-37, spectrin-strut-38, spectrin-strut-39, spectrin-strut-40, spectrin-strut-41, spectrin-strut-42, spectrin-strut-43, spectrin-strut-44, spectrin-strut-45, spectrin-strut-46, spectrin-strut-47, spectrin-strut-48, spectrin-strut-49, spectrin-strut-50, spectrin-strut-51, spectrin-strut-52, spectrin-strut-53, spectrin-strut-54, spectrin-strut-55, spectrin-strut-56, spectrin-strut-57, spectrin-strut-58, spectrin-strut-59, spectrin-node-0, spectrin-node-1, spectrin-node-2, spectrin-node-3, spectrin-node-4, spectrin-node-5, spectrin-node-6, spectrin-node-7, spectrin-node-8, spectrin-node-9): A flexible sub-membrane filamentous network built from spectrin tetramers linked to short actin junctions. Function: Maintains the erythrocyte's biconcave shape and gives the membrane elastic reversibility after squeezing through microvessels.
    - Fact: A filamentous meshwork of spectrin underlies the red blood cell plasma membrane and is essential for maintaining the cell's biconcave shape and deformability. [National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI Bookshelf), Chapter 10, 'Membrane Structure' (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK21054/)]
    - Fact: Spectrin filaments are linked at junctional complexes containing short actin filaments and anchored to integral membrane proteins. [National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI Bookshelf), Chapter 10, 'Membrane Structure' (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK21054/)]
  - **Hemoglobin cytoplasm** (high confidence; meshes: hemoglobin-matrix, hemoglobin-tetramer-rim, hemoglobin-tetramer-inner): Dense, iron-rich tetrameric metalloproteins occupying nearly the entire interior of the mature erythrocyte. Function: Reversibly binds oxygen in the lungs and releases it to respiring tissues while buffering protons and assisting CO₂ transport.
    - Fact: Mature mammalian red blood cells lack a nucleus and mitochondria, leaving most of their internal volume filled with hemoglobin. [OpenStax, §18.3, 'Erythrocytes' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/18-3-erythrocytes)]
    - Fact: Each hemoglobin tetramer carries four iron-containing heme groups that reversibly bind oxygen. [OpenStax, §18.3, 'Hemoglobin' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/18-3-erythrocytes)]
  - **Membrane transporters** (high confidence; meshes: membrane-transporter-0, membrane-transporter-1, membrane-transporter-2, membrane-transporter-3, membrane-transporter-4, membrane-transporter-5, membrane-transporter-6, membrane-transporter-7): Abundant transmembrane protein channels, including Band 3 anion exchangers and aquaporin water pores. Function: Rapidly swap bicarbonate and chloride ions (the chloride shift) and equilibrate water across the membrane.
    - Fact: Band 3 is an abundant integral anion-exchange protein in the erythrocyte membrane that swaps chloride and bicarbonate ions across the bilayer. [National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI Bookshelf), Chapter 10, 'Membrane Structure' (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK21054/)]
    - Fact: Bicarbonate formed inside erythrocytes leaves via membrane exchange proteins so carbon dioxide is transported efficiently in blood plasma. [OpenStax, §18.3, 'Hemoglobin' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/18-3-erythrocytes)]
  - **Carbonic anhydrase** (high confidence; meshes: carbonic-anhydrase): A cytosolic enzyme that catalyses the rapid interconversion of carbon dioxide and water with carbonic acid and bicarbonate. Function: Accelerates tissue CO₂ uptake into red blood cells and its conversion back to exhaled CO₂ in pulmonary capillaries.
    - Fact: Carbonic anhydrase inside erythrocytes catalyses the rapid reversible hydration of carbon dioxide into carbonic acid, which dissociates into bicarbonate and hydrogen ions. [OpenStax, §18.3, 'Hemoglobin' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/18-3-erythrocytes)]
    - Fact: Without erythrocyte carbonic anhydrase, the conversion between dissolved carbon dioxide and bicarbonate would proceed far too slowly during capillary transit. [Encyclopaedia Britannica, Introduction, 'Red blood cell' (https://www.britannica.com/science/red-blood-cell)]
  - **Surface glycocalyx** (high confidence; meshes: glycocalyx-stalk-0, glycocalyx-sugar-0, glycocalyx-stalk-1, glycocalyx-sugar-1, glycocalyx-stalk-2, glycocalyx-sugar-2, glycocalyx-stalk-3, glycocalyx-sugar-3, glycocalyx-stalk-4, glycocalyx-sugar-4, glycocalyx-stalk-5, glycocalyx-sugar-5, glycocalyx-stalk-6, glycocalyx-sugar-6, glycocalyx-stalk-7, glycocalyx-sugar-7, glycocalyx-stalk-8, glycocalyx-sugar-8, glycocalyx-stalk-9, glycocalyx-sugar-9, glycocalyx-stalk-10, glycocalyx-sugar-10, glycocalyx-stalk-11, glycocalyx-sugar-11, glycocalyx-stalk-12, glycocalyx-sugar-12, glycocalyx-stalk-13, glycocalyx-sugar-13): A negatively charged coat of glycoproteins and glycolipids extending from the outer leaflet of the plasma membrane. Function: Carries ABO and Rh blood-group antigens and creates electrostatic repulsion that prevents cells from clumping in vessels.
    - Fact: Red blood cell surface glycoproteins and glycolipids carry carbohydrate chains that define ABO blood-group antigens. [OpenStax, §18.3, 'Erythrocytes' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/18-3-erythrocytes)]
    - Fact: Cell-surface carbohydrate chains form a protective glycocalyx on the noncytosolic face of animal plasma membranes. [National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI Bookshelf), Chapter 10, 'Membrane Structure' (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK21054/)]

### Yeast cell (Saccharomyces cerevisiae)

- **Domain / Cell type**: fungi · Budding unicellular fungus
- **Size & scale**: Roughly 5–10 µm diameter — Schematic and unitless. Cell-wall layers, pore rings, and dispersed Golgi cisternae are scaled for clarity.
- **3D stats**: 70 mesh instances · ~20,072 estimated triangles · Capabilities: 3D procedural mesh, Structure camera focus, Cutaway shell toggle, Mesh-mapped highlighting, PNG screenshot export, GLB export capability · Preview: `/previews/yeast-cell.svg`
- **Summary**: A budding unicellular eukaryote with a chitin-glucan cell wall, chitinous bud scars, fungal vacuole, and polarised secretory growth into a daughter bud.
- **Overview**: Saccharomyces cerevisiae combines features familiar from other eukaryotes with distinctly fungal traits: a rigid wall rich in chitin and glucans rather than cellulose or peptidoglycan, a large vacuole that functions like a plant tonoplast and animal lysosome, and asymmetric cell division by budding. This schematic captures a mother cell forming an emerging daughter bud along with chitin rings left by prior divisions.
- **Traits**: Nucleus: Present | Cell wall: Present (chitin and glucans) | Chloroplasts: Absent | Motility: Non-motile | Typical size: 5–10 µm | Organisation: Eukaryotic, unicellular fungus
- **Structures (7)**:
  - **Chitin–glucan cell wall** (high confidence; meshes: cell-wall-mother, cell-wall-bud, bud-neck-ring, bud-scar-a, bud-scar-b): A tough polysaccharide wall made of glucans, mannoproteins, and chitin that encloses both mother cell and bud. Function: Resists osmotic lysis, maintains ovoid shape, and concentrates chitin in the bud-neck septum and persistent bud scars.
    - Fact: Fungal cell walls contain chitin and glucans—structural polysaccharides distinct from the cellulose of plant cell walls and the peptidoglycan of bacteria. [OpenStax, §24.1, 'Cell Structure and Function' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/24-1-characteristics-of-fungi)]
    - Fact: Most yeasts divide asexually by budding, leaving circular chitin-rich bud scars where a daughter cell pinched off. [Encyclopaedia Britannica, Introduction, 'Yeast' (https://www.britannica.com/science/yeast-fungus)]
  - **Plasma membrane** (high confidence; meshes: plasma-membrane-mother, plasma-membrane-bud): A phospholipid bilayer containing ergosterol beneath the fungal cell wall that regulates transport. Function: Mediates nutrient uptake, ion gradients, and exocytosis of new cell-wall components into the growing bud.
    - Fact: The plasma membrane is a phospholipid bilayer containing transport and signalling proteins that sits inside the cell wall. [OpenStax, §4.3, 'The Plasma Membrane' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-3-eukaryotic-cells)]
    - Fact: Unlike animal cell membranes which contain cholesterol, fungal plasma membranes use ergosterol to help stabilise the bilayer. [OpenStax, §24.1, 'Cell Structure and Function' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/24-1-characteristics-of-fungi)]
  - **Nucleus** (high confidence; meshes: nucleus, nucleus-chromatin, nucleolus, nuclear-pore): A double-membrane organelle housing yeast chromosomes inside a nuclear envelope that remains intact during mitosis. Function: Coordinates gene expression and migrates toward the bud neck prior to nuclear division.
    - Fact: Like all eukaryotes, yeast cells enclose their chromosomal DNA within a nuclear envelope studded with nuclear pores. [OpenStax, §4.3, 'The Nucleus' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-3-eukaryotic-cells)]
    - Fact: Fungi typically undergo closed mitosis, dividing chromatin within an intact nuclear envelope rather than breaking it down. [OpenStax, §24.1, 'Reproduction' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/24-1-characteristics-of-fungi)]
  - **Fungal vacuole** (high confidence; meshes: vacuole-mother, vacuole-bud): An acidic membrane-bound compartment analogous to both lysosomes and plant vacuoles. Function: Stores amino acids and polyphosphate, maintains cytosolic pH, and degrades macromolecules via hydrolytic enzymes.
    - Fact: In fungi such as yeast, the vacuole carries out degradative and storage roles analogous to lysosomes in animal cells. [OpenStax, §4.3, 'Vacuoles' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-3-eukaryotic-cells)]
    - Fact: Yeast vacuoles serve as dynamic reservoirs of ions and metabolites and split material into the growing daughter bud. [National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI Bookshelf), Chapter 13, 'Intracellular Vesicular Traffic' (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK21054/)]
  - **Mitochondrion** (high confidence; meshes: mitochondrion-0, mitochondrion-cristae-0, mitochondrion-1, mitochondrion-cristae-1, mitochondrion-2, mitochondrion-cristae-2, mitochondrion-3, mitochondrion-cristae-3): A dynamic cortical network of double-membrane organelles powering aerobic ATP production. Function: Generates ATP during oxidative respiration and partitions along actin cables into the emerging bud.
    - Fact: Mitochondria produce ATP by aerobic respiration using an inner membrane folded into cristae. [OpenStax, §4.3, 'Mitochondria' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-3-eukaryotic-cells)]
    - Fact: Yeast cells are facultative anaerobes that rely on mitochondrial respiration when oxygen is available and ferment sugars when it is scarce. [Encyclopaedia Britannica, Introduction, 'Yeast' (https://www.britannica.com/science/yeast-fungus)]
  - **Endoplasmic reticulum** (high confidence; meshes: er-sheet-0, er-sheet-1, er-sheet-2, er-sheet-3, er-ribosome): Ribosome-studded perinuclear and cortical membrane sheets continuous with the outer nuclear envelope. Function: Synthesises secretory proteins, cell-wall synthases, and membrane lipids needed for cell growth.
    - Fact: The endoplasmic reticulum forms a continuous membrane system from the nuclear envelope through the cytoplasm to produce proteins and lipids. [OpenStax, §4.4, 'The Endoplasmic Reticulum' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-4-the-endomembrane-system-and-proteins)]
    - Fact: Ribosomes bound to ER membranes translate nascent secretory and membrane proteins directly into the ER lumen or bilayer. [OpenStax, §4.4, 'The Endoplasmic Reticulum' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-4-the-endomembrane-system-and-proteins)]
  - **Dispersed Golgi & vesicles** (high confidence; meshes: golgi-cisterna-0, golgi-cisterna-1, golgi-cisterna-2, golgi-secretory-vesicle): Unstacked Golgi cisternae distributed through the cytoplasm rather than clustered in one ribbon. Function: Sorts glycoproteins and aims secretory vesicles along actin cables into the expanding daughter bud.
    - Fact: The Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts, and packages proteins and lipids into transport vesicles. [OpenStax, §4.4, 'The Golgi Apparatus' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-4-the-endomembrane-system-and-proteins)]
    - Fact: Unlike mammalian cells with a single perinuclear Golgi stack, budding yeast keep individual Golgi cisternae dispersed throughout the cytoplasm. [National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI Bookshelf), Chapter 13, 'Intracellular Vesicular Traffic' (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK21054/)]

### Paramecium (Paramecium caudatum)

- **Domain / Cell type**: protist · Freshwater ciliate protist
- **Size & scale**: Roughly 120–300 µm long — Schematic and unitless. Cilia rows are thinned from real densities and internal organelles are spaced so their roles stay legible.
- **3D stats**: 101 mesh instances · ~31,296 estimated triangles · Capabilities: 3D procedural mesh, Structure camera focus, Cutaway shell toggle, Mesh-mapped highlighting, PNG screenshot export, GLB export capability · Preview: `/previews/paramecium.svg`
- **Summary**: A ciliated unicellular protist with a flexible pellicle, oral feeding groove, dual macro- and micronucleus, and star-shaped contractile vacuoles.
- **Overview**: Paramecium caudatum is a complex single-celled eukaryote that carries out feeding, locomotion, osmotic water balancers, and sexual exchange inside one cell. Rows of coordinated cilia propel the slipper-shaped cell through pond water while an oral groove sweeps bacteria into food vacuoles. Inside, star-shaped contractile vacuoles pump out incoming osmotic water, and two distinct nuclei divide genetic labor. Geometry is schematic and proportions are exaggerated for clarity.
- **Traits**: Nucleus: Present; dual (macro- and micronucleus) | Cell wall: Absent (flexible pellicle) | Chloroplasts: Absent | Motility: Ciliated swimming | Typical size: 120–300 µm | Organisation: Eukaryotic, unicellular ciliate protist
- **Structures (7)**:
  - **Pellicle** (high confidence; meshes: pellicle-body, pellicle-posterior): A flexible yet supportive outer cortex formed by the plasma membrane backed by flattened alveolar sacs and cytoskeletal fibres. Function: Maintains the streamlined slipper contour while allowing elastic bending around obstacles.
    - Fact: Many protists, including ciliates like Paramecium, have a flexible outer pellicle made of interlocking protein strips and membrane alveoli beneath the plasma membrane. [OpenStax, §23.3, 'Alveolates: Dinoflagellates, Apicomplexans, and Ciliates' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/23-3-groups-of-protists)]
    - Fact: The Paramecium pellicle sustains a characteristic slipper shape while still flexing when colliding with barriers. [Encyclopaedia Britannica, Introduction, 'Paramecium' (https://www.britannica.com/science/Paramecium)]
  - **Cilia** (high confidence; meshes: cilium-0, cilium-1, cilium-2, cilium-3, cilium-4, cilium-5, cilium-6, cilium-7, cilium-8, cilium-9, cilium-10, cilium-11, cilium-12, cilium-13, cilium-14, cilium-15, cilium-16, cilium-17, cilium-18, cilium-19, cilium-20, cilium-21, cilium-22, cilium-23, cilium-24, cilium-25, cilium-26, cilium-27, cilium-28, cilium-29, cilium-30, cilium-31, cilium-32, cilium-33, cilium-34, cilium-35, cilium-36, cilium-37, cilium-38, cilium-39, cilium-40, cilium-41, cilium-42, cilium-43, cilium-44, cilium-45, cilium-46, cilium-47, cilium-48, cilium-49, cilium-50, cilium-51, cilium-52, cilium-53, cilium-54, cilium-55, cilium-56, cilium-57, cilium-58, cilium-59): Hundreds of short, hair-like microtubule-based organelles beating in coordinated waves across the pellicle. Function: Propel the cell along a helical path and reverse stroke direction quickly in avoiding reactions.
    - Fact: Ciliates use coordinated rows of short hair-like cilia driven by dynein motors on 9+2 microtubule doublets to swim through water. [OpenStax, §23.3, 'Alveolates: Dinoflagellates, Apicomplexans, and Ciliates' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/23-3-groups-of-protists)]
    - Fact: Cilia and eukaryotic flagella share an internal axoneme of nine outer microtubule doublets surrounding a central pair. [OpenStax, §4.5, 'Flagella and Cilia' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-5-the-cytoskeleton)]
  - **Oral groove & cytostome** (high confidence; meshes: oral-groove-channel, oral-cytostome, oral-cytopharynx, oral-cilium-0, oral-cilium-1, oral-cilium-2, oral-cilium-3, oral-cilium-4, oral-cilium-5): A ciliated ventral channel funneling suspended microbes inward toward the cell mouth (cytostome) and gullet. Function: Directs a feeding water current toward the cytostome, where particles are packaged into nascent food vacuoles.
    - Fact: Paramecium captures food using an oral groove lined with beating cilia that sweep bacteria toward a primitive cell mouth (cytostome). [OpenStax, §23.3, 'Alveolates: Dinoflagellates, Apicomplexans, and Ciliates' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/23-3-groups-of-protists)]
    - Fact: Food particles concentrated at the base of the gullet are enclosed in membrane-bound food vacuoles pinched off into the cytoplasm. [Encyclopaedia Britannica, Introduction, 'Paramecium' (https://www.britannica.com/science/Paramecium)]
  - **Macronucleus** (high confidence; meshes: macronucleus-anterior, macronucleus-posterior, macronucleus-chromatin): A large, kidney-shaped polyploid nucleus containing numerous amplified copies of somatic genes. Function: Directs everyday transcription, metabolism, and vegetative growth across the large protist cell.
    - Fact: Ciliates exhibit nuclear dimorphism, carrying a large polyploid macronucleus that handles everyday metabolic gene expression. [OpenStax, §23.3, 'Alveolates: Dinoflagellates, Apicomplexans, and Ciliates' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/23-3-groups-of-protists)]
    - Fact: During asexual fission the Paramecium macronucleus elongates and divides amitotically to supply both daughter cells. [Encyclopaedia Britannica, Introduction, 'Paramecium' (https://www.britannica.com/science/Paramecium)]
  - **Micronucleus** (high confidence; meshes: micronucleus): A small, diploid germline nucleus tucked close to the concave notch of the macronucleus. Function: Preserves the complete germline genome and exchanges haploid micronuclei during sexual conjugation.
    - Fact: Alongside the macronucleus, ciliates possess one or more compact diploid micronuclei specialised for genetic recombination during conjugation. [OpenStax, §23.3, 'Alveolates: Dinoflagellates, Apicomplexans, and Ciliates' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/23-3-groups-of-protists)]
    - Fact: While the macronucleus degrades after conjugation, the synkaryon derived from micronuclear exchange generates a new macronucleus. [Encyclopaedia Britannica, Introduction, 'Paramecium' (https://www.britannica.com/science/Paramecium)]
  - **Contractile vacuoles** (high confidence; meshes: cv-bladder-0, cv-bladder-1, cv-canal-0-0, cv-canal-0-1, cv-canal-0-2, cv-canal-0-3, cv-canal-0-4, cv-canal-0-5, cv-canal-1-0, cv-canal-1-1, cv-canal-1-2, cv-canal-1-3, cv-canal-1-4, cv-canal-1-5): Two star-shaped osmoregulatory organelles with radiating collecting canals at the anterior and posterior ends. Function: Continuously collect and pump excess water diffusing in from hypotonic pond water back outside the cell.
    - Fact: Freshwater Paramecium cells use two contractile vacuoles fed by radiating collecting canals to expel excess water absorbed by osmosis and prevent bursting. [OpenStax, §23.3, 'Alveolates: Dinoflagellates, Apicomplexans, and Ciliates' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/23-3-groups-of-protists)]
    - Fact: Amoeboid and ciliated protists in freshwater maintain osmotic balance with rhythmic cycles of diastole filling and systole contraction. [National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI Bookshelf), Chapter 11, 'Membrane Transport of Small Molecules and the Electrical Properties of Membranes' (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK21054/)]
  - **Food vacuoles** (high confidence; meshes: food-vacuole-0, food-vacuole-content-0, food-vacuole-1, food-vacuole-content-1, food-vacuole-2, food-vacuole-content-2, food-vacuole-3, food-vacuole-content-3, food-vacuole-4, food-vacuole-content-4, food-vacuole-5, food-vacuole-content-5): Membrane-bound digestive vesicles enclosing ingested microbes as they circulate through the cytoplasm. Function: Acidify, fuse with digestive enzymes, and deliver absorbed nutrients along cytoplasmic streaming (cyclosis) paths.
    - Fact: Newly formed food vacuoles circulate through Paramecium cytoplasm as lysosomal enzymes digest engulfed bacteria. [Encyclopaedia Britannica, Introduction, 'Paramecium' (https://www.britannica.com/science/Paramecium)]
    - Fact: Undigested residues are eventually discharged when spent food vacuoles fuse with a specialised region of the pellicle (the cytoproct). [OpenStax, §23.3, 'Alveolates: Dinoflagellates, Apicomplexans, and Ciliates' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/23-3-groups-of-protists)]

### Human brain (Homo sapiens)

- **Domain / Cell type**: animal · Central nervous system organ (intact 3D)
- **Size & scale**: Roughly 140 × 170 × 110 mm; ~1.3–1.4 kg — Schematic and unitless. Gyri, sulcal depths, and regional borders are stylised for clarity and cannot be used as clinical neuroimaging coordinates.
- **3D stats**: 25 mesh instances · ~32,000 estimated triangles · Capabilities: 3D procedural mesh, Structure camera focus, Cutaway shell toggle, Mesh-mapped highlighting, PNG screenshot export, GLB export capability · Preview: `/previews/human-brain.svg`
- **Summary**: An interactive whole-brain 3D model divided into functional cortical lobes, cerebellum, and brainstem, with a cutaway exposing the corpus callosum and limbic core.
- **Overview**: The human brain coordinates perception, voluntary movement, language, emotion, memory, and autonomic survival across specialised cortical lobes and subcortical hubs. Here, both cerebral hemispheres display folded gyri and sulci coloured by major anatomical and functional divisions—frontal, primary motor, primary somatosensory, parietal, temporal, and occipital—above the striated cerebellum and brainstem. Toggle Cutaway to remove the right cortical hemisphere and inspect the corpus callosum and deep limbic structures nestled inside.
- **Traits**: Nucleus: Multicellular organ (~86 billion neurons) | Cell wall: Absent (meninges & cranium) | Chloroplasts: Absent | Motility: Non-motile; coordinates motor output | Typical size: ~140 × 170 × 110 mm (~1.3–1.4 kg) | Organisation: Central nervous system organ, bilateral
- **Structures (10)**:
  - **Frontal lobe** (high confidence; meshes: frontal-lobe-right, frontal-lobe-left): The anterior cortical lobe governing executive planning, decision-making, working memory, and speech production. Function: Integrates prefrontal executive control, impulse inhibition, and anterior language circuits (such as Broca's area in the dominant hemisphere).
    - Fact: The frontal lobe sits anterior to the central sulcus and houses prefrontal circuits responsible for executive functions, attention, and planning. [OpenStax, §13.2, 'The Cerebrum' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/13-2-the-central-nervous-system)]
    - Fact: The frontal lobe coordinates higher cognitive processing, judgment, and motor speech output. [OpenStax, §35.3, 'Brain: Cerebral Cortex' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/35-3-the-central-nervous-system)]
  - **Primary motor cortex** (high confidence; meshes: motor-lobe-right, motor-lobe-left): The precentral gyrus immediately anterior to the central sulcus that initiates voluntary skeletal movements. Function: Maps contralateral body musculature somatotopically and projects upper motor neuron commands down the corticospinal tract.
    - Fact: The primary motor cortex occupies the precentral gyrus of the frontal lobe and sends descending commands for voluntary skeletal movement. [OpenStax, §13.2, 'The Cerebrum' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/13-2-the-central-nervous-system)]
    - Fact: Each hemisphere's primary motor cortex predominantly controls voluntary musculature on the opposite side of the body. [Encyclopaedia Britannica, Section 'Cerebral cortex' (https://www.britannica.com/science/human-brain)]
  - **Primary somatosensory cortex** (high confidence; meshes: sensory-lobe-right, sensory-lobe-left): The postcentral gyrus immediately posterior to the central sulcus that receives touch, pressure, pain, and proprioceptive signals. Function: Maps tactile and proprioceptive inputs from contralateral body regions after relay through the thalamus.
    - Fact: The primary somatosensory cortex lies in the postcentral gyrus of the parietal lobe and processes general sensory information from skin and joints. [OpenStax, §13.2, 'The Cerebrum' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/13-2-the-central-nervous-system)]
