    - Fact: Cortical surface area in the somatosensory map reflects sensory receptor density rather than anatomical body size. [OpenStax, §35.3, 'Brain: Cerebral Cortex' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/35-3-the-central-nervous-system)]
  - **Parietal lobe** (high confidence; meshes: parietal-lobe-right, parietal-lobe-left): The superior-posterior lobe behind the postcentral gyrus that integrates spatial awareness, multisensory perception, and reading. Function: Combines tactile, visual, and proprioceptive cues to construct body schema and spatial attention.
    - Fact: The parietal lobe sits posterior to the central sulcus and integrates somatosensory perception with spatial navigation. [OpenStax, §13.2, 'The Cerebrum' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/13-2-the-central-nervous-system)]
    - Fact: Association regions in the parietal cortex help evaluate object shape, texture, and spatial orientation. [Encyclopaedia Britannica, Section 'Lobes of the cerebral cortex' (https://www.britannica.com/science/human-brain)]
  - **Temporal lobe** (high confidence; meshes: temporal-lobe-right, temporal-lobe-left): The inferior lateral lobe beneath the lateral sulcus housing primary auditory cortex, speech comprehension, and memory interfaces. Function: Processes auditory signals, links spoken language in Wernicke's area, and connects closely with deep medial memory structures.
    - Fact: Separated from the frontal and parietal lobes by the lateral sulcus, the temporal lobe processes auditory perception and language comprehension. [OpenStax, §13.2, 'The Cerebrum' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/13-2-the-central-nervous-system)]
    - Fact: Medial temporal lobe regions work closely with the hippocampus and amygdala in memory and emotional association. [OpenStax, §35.3, 'Brain: Cerebral Cortex' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/35-3-the-central-nervous-system)]
  - **Occipital lobe** (high confidence; meshes: occipital-lobe-right, occipital-lobe-left): The posterior cortical lobe above the cerebellum dedicated to primary visual reception and visual association. Function: Decodes retinotopic orientation, motion, colour, and spatial form delivered from the optic tracts via the thalamus.
    - Fact: The occipital lobe forms the posterior pole of the cerebrum and contains the primary visual cortex for interpreting visual input. [OpenStax, §13.2, 'The Cerebrum' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/13-2-the-central-nervous-system)]
    - Fact: Visual association areas in the occipital lobe link raw visual features with memory and object recognition. [OpenStax, §35.3, 'Brain: Cerebral Cortex' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/35-3-the-central-nervous-system)]
  - **Cerebellum** (high confidence; meshes: cerebellum-right, cerebellum-left, cerebellum-vermis): The densely folded 'little brain' tucked beneath the occipital lobes posterior to the pons. Function: Compares motor plans with proprioceptive feedback to smooth posture, balance, timing, and coordinated movement.
    - Fact: The cerebellum coordinates posture, balance, and precise timing of skeletal muscle contractions by comparing motor intent with sensory feedback. [OpenStax, §13.2, 'The Cerebellum' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/13-2-the-central-nervous-system)]
    - Fact: Although smaller in volume than the cerebrum, the cerebellum has a tightly folded cortex (folia) packed with neurons. [Encyclopaedia Britannica, Section 'Cerebellum' (https://www.britannica.com/science/human-brain)]
  - **Brainstem** (high confidence; meshes: brainstem): The midline stalk comprising the midbrain, pons, and medulla oblongata linking forebrain and cerebellum to the spinal cord. Function: Routes ascending and descending nerve tracts while sustaining essential autonomic breathing, heart rate, and blood pressure reflexes.
    - Fact: The brainstem consists of the midbrain, pons, and medulla oblongata and houses cardiovascular and respiratory centres vital for survival. [OpenStax, §13.2, 'The Brain Stem' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/13-2-the-central-nervous-system)]
    - Fact: Cranial nerve nuclei and major ascending sensory and descending motor tracts pass through the brainstem between the brain and spinal cord. [OpenStax, §35.3, 'Brain: Brainstem' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/35-3-the-central-nervous-system)]
  - **Corpus callosum** (high confidence; meshes: corpus-callosum): The thick C-shaped commissural tract of myelinated axons bridging the left and right cerebral hemispheres. Function: Allows continuous interhemispheric communication so both halves of the cortex share sensory, motor, and cognitive processing.
    - Fact: The corpus callosum is the largest white-matter commissure in the human brain, connecting corresponding regions of both cerebral hemispheres. [OpenStax, §13.2, 'The Cerebrum' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/13-2-the-central-nervous-system)]
    - Fact: Millions of myelinated axons cross the midline through the corpus callosum to coordinate bilateral brain activity. [OpenStax, §35.3, 'Brain: Cerebral Cortex' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/35-3-the-central-nervous-system)]
  - **Deep limbic & thalamic core** (high confidence; meshes: thalamus-right, thalamus-left, hippocampus-right, hippocampus-left, amygdala-right, amygdala-left, fornix-right, fornix-left): Subcortical relay and limbic structures (thalamus, hippocampus, amygdala, and fornix) enclosed beneath the cerebral cortex. Function: Relays sensory information to the cortex while driving emotional processing, threat appraisal, and long-term memory consolidation.
    - Fact: The thalamus relays nearly all sensory pathways (except olfaction) toward the cerebral cortex, while the limbic system links emotion and memory. [OpenStax, §13.2, 'The Diencephalon' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/13-2-the-central-nervous-system)]
    - Fact: Subcortical structures including the hippocampus, amygdala, and fornix form interconnected loops for declarative memory and affective responses. [Encyclopaedia Britannica, Introduction, 'Limbic system' (https://www.britannica.com/science/limbic-system)]

### Human brain (cutout) (Homo sapiens)

- **Domain / Cell type**: animal · Sagittal & limbic neuroanatomy cutout
- **Size & scale**: Roughly 140 × 170 × 110 mm (open cutaway) — Schematic and unitless. Deep nuclei, ventricles, and cranial nerves are spaced slightly for visual separation and interactive picking rather than surgical precision.
- **3D stats**: 39 mesh instances · ~26,430 estimated triangles · Capabilities: 3D procedural mesh, Structure camera focus, Cutaway shell toggle, Mesh-mapped highlighting, PNG screenshot export, GLB export capability · Preview: `/previews/human-brain-cutout.svg`
- **Summary**: An open anatomical brain cutout exposing the limbic system (hippocampus, amygdala, cingulate gyrus, fornix), thalamus, hypothalamus, ventricles, and brainstem.
- **Overview**: Removing the right cortical shell reveals the tightly layered architecture beneath the cerebral cortex. Along the midline sit the corpus callosum, thalamus, hypothalamus, pituitary gland, ventricular cavities, brainstem, and cerebellum, framed by the C-shaped limbic system—cingulate gyrus, fornix, hippocampus, and amygdala—that links emotion, motivation, and long-term memory. Toggle Cutaway to hide the remaining left cortical hemisphere and view the subcortical organs in isolation.
- **Traits**: Nucleus: Multicellular organ (~86 billion neurons) | Cell wall: Absent (meninges & CSF ventricles) | Chloroplasts: Absent | Motility: Non-motile; integrates limbic & motor circuits | Typical size: ~140 × 170 × 110 mm (sagittal cutout) | Organisation: Central nervous system organ, subcortical view
- **Structures (12)**:
  - **Cerebral cortex (cutaway hemisphere)** (high confidence; meshes: cutout-left-hemisphere): The folded outer grey matter of the retained left cerebral hemisphere forming a sagittal shell around the deep brain. Function: Carries out conscious perception, language, reasoning, and voluntary motor planning across its gyri and sulci.
    - Fact: The cerebral cortex is a heavily folded sheet of grey matter whose gyri (ridges) and sulci (grooves) greatly expand cortical surface area within the skull. [OpenStax, §13.2, 'The Cerebrum' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/13-2-the-central-nervous-system)]
    - Fact: Beneath the cortical grey matter lies subcortical white matter carrying axons between cortical areas and deep nuclei. [OpenStax, §35.3, 'Brain: Cerebral Cortex' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/35-3-the-central-nervous-system)]
  - **Corpus callosum** (high confidence; meshes: corpus-callosum): The broad C-shaped white-matter commissure (rostrum, genu, body, and splenium) bridging left and right hemispheres. Function: Transfers sensory, motor, and cognitive information rapidly across the cerebral midline.
    - Fact: The corpus callosum is a thick band of myelinated commissural fibres connecting the left and right cerebral hemispheres. [OpenStax, §13.2, 'The Cerebrum' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/13-2-the-central-nervous-system)]
    - Fact: In sagittal view the corpus callosum forms an arch directly above the lateral ventricles and thalamus. [Encyclopaedia Britannica, Section 'Cerebrum' (https://www.britannica.com/science/human-brain)]
  - **Cingulate gyrus (limbic cortex)** (high confidence; meshes: cingulate-gyrus-right, cingulate-gyrus-left): The arching cortical rim wrapping immediately dorsal to the corpus callosum along the medial hemisphere wall. Function: Integrates emotional appraisal, pain processing, conflict monitoring, and autonomic regulation within the limbic circuit.
    - Fact: The cingulate gyrus forms part of the limbic cortex encircling the corpus callosum and participates in emotion and behaviour regulation. [OpenStax, §13.2, 'The Cerebrum' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/13-2-the-central-nervous-system)]
    - Fact: Limbic cortical pathways connect the cingulate gyrus with the hippocampus, amygdala, and prefrontal cortex. [Encyclopaedia Britannica, Introduction, 'Limbic system' (https://www.britannica.com/science/limbic-system)]
  - **Hippocampus** (high confidence; meshes: hippocampus-right, hippocampus-left): A curved, seahorse-shaped medial temporal lobe structure central to forming new declarative memories. Function: Consolidates short-term experiences into long-term episodic and spatial memories before routing output via the fornix.
    - Fact: Located in the medial temporal lobe, the hippocampus is essential for consolidating short-term experience into long-term declarative memory. [OpenStax, §13.2, 'The Cerebrum' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/13-2-the-central-nervous-system)]
    - Fact: The hippocampus projects along the arching fimbria and fornix toward the mammillary bodies and anterior thalamus. [Encyclopaedia Britannica, Section 'Hippocampus and memory' (https://www.britannica.com/science/limbic-system)]
  - **Amygdala** (high confidence; meshes: amygdala-right, amygdala-left): Almond-shaped nuclear complexes sitting immediately anterior to the head of each hippocampus in the temporal lobe. Function: Evaluates emotional salience—especially fear, threat, and reward—and modulates autonomic arousal and emotional memory.
    - Fact: The amygdala is a deep temporal-lobe nucleus of the limbic system involved in fear processing, emotional significance, and affective memory. [OpenStax, §35.3, 'Brain: Limbic System' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/35-3-the-central-nervous-system)]
    - Fact: Positioned just ahead of the hippocampus, the amygdala connects strongly with the hypothalamus and brainstem autonomic centres. [Encyclopaedia Britannica, Section 'Amygdala' (https://www.britannica.com/science/limbic-system)]
  - **Fornix & mammillary bodies** (high confidence; meshes: fornix-right, fornix-left, mammillary-right, mammillary-left, anterior-commissure): An arched white-matter fibre bundle carrying hippocampal output beneath the corpus callosum down to the mammillary bodies. Function: Links the hippocampus with the hypothalamus and anterior thalamic nuclei as part of the Papez memory circuit.
    - Fact: The fornix is a C-shaped tract of myelinated axons that conducts signals from the hippocampus around the thalamus to the mammillary bodies. [Encyclopaedia Britannica, Introduction, 'Limbic system' (https://www.britannica.com/science/limbic-system)]
    - Fact: Mammillary bodies at the inferior-posterior boundary of the hypothalamus serve as relay nuclei for memory circuits. [OpenStax, §13.2, 'The Diencephalon' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/13-2-the-central-nervous-system)]
  - **Thalamus** (high confidence; meshes: thalamus-right, thalamus-left, interthalamic-adhesion): Paired egg-shaped grey-matter relay hubs forming the dorsal diencephalon on either side of the third ventricle. Function: Filters, integrates, and relays ascending sensory and motor feedback signals to specific regions of the cerebral cortex.
    - Fact: The thalamus acts as a major relay and processing station for almost all sensory inputs (except olfaction) heading to the cerebral cortex. [OpenStax, §13.2, 'The Diencephalon' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/13-2-the-central-nervous-system)]
    - Fact: Two large thalamic masses flank the third ventricle and are often bridged across the midline by the interthalamic adhesion. [Encyclopaedia Britannica, Section 'Diencephalon' (https://www.britannica.com/science/human-brain)]
  - **Hypothalamus & pituitary gland** (high confidence; meshes: hypothalamus, infundibulum, pituitary-anterior, pituitary-posterior): The ventral diencephalic homeostatic regulator connected via the infundibulum stalk to the endocrine pituitary gland. Function: Maintains body temperature, hunger, thirst, circadian rhythms, autonomic balance, and neuroendocrine hormone release.
    - Fact: The hypothalamus sits inferior and anterior to the thalamus and acts as the master coordinator of homeostasis, autonomic output, and endocrine control via the pituitary gland. [OpenStax, §13.2, 'The Diencephalon' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/13-2-the-central-nervous-system)]
    - Fact: The pituitary gland attaches to the hypothalamus by the infundibulum and secretes hormones governing growth, stress, reproduction, and water balance. [OpenStax, §35.3, 'Brain: Diencephalon' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/35-3-the-central-nervous-system)]
  - **Cerebral ventricles** (high confidence; meshes: lateral-ventricle-right, lateral-ventricle-left, third-ventricle, cerebral-aqueduct, fourth-ventricle): The interconnected fluid-filled chambers (lateral, third, cerebral aqueduct, and fourth ventricles) containing cerebrospinal fluid. Function: Produce and circulate cerebrospinal fluid via choroid plexuses to buoy, cushion, and chemically bathe the central nervous system.
    - Fact: Four interconnected brain ventricles house choroid plexuses that secrete cerebrospinal fluid to cushion and support the brain. [OpenStax, §13.3, 'Cerebrospinal Fluid' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/13-3-circulation-and-the-central-nervous-system)]
    - Fact: CSF flows from the lateral ventricles into the midline third ventricle, down the cerebral aqueduct, and into the fourth ventricle between pons and cerebellum. [OpenStax, §35.3, 'Brain: Meninges and Ventricles' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/35-3-the-central-nervous-system)]
  - **Olfactory bulbs & optic nerves** (high confidence; meshes: olfactory-tract-right, olfactory-tract-left, olfactory-bulb-right, olfactory-bulb-left, optic-chiasm, optic-nerve-right, optic-nerve-left, optic-tract-right, optic-tract-left): Anterior ventral sensory pathways: olfactory bulbs/tracts (CN I) beneath the frontal lobe and optic nerves/chiasm (CN II). Function: Convey smell directly to olfactory cortex and limbic centres, while routing visual input from the retinas through the optic chiasm.
    - Fact: Olfactory bulbs lie beneath the frontal lobes and transmit smell signals without a mandatory thalamic relay directly to cortical and limbic areas. [OpenStax, §13.2, 'The Cerebrum' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/13-2-the-central-nervous-system)]
    - Fact: Optic nerves converge at the optic chiasm anterior to the pituitary stalk before continuing as optic tracts toward the thalamus. [Encyclopaedia Britannica, Section 'Cranial nerves and sensory pathways' (https://www.britannica.com/science/human-brain)]
  - **Cerebellum** (high confidence; meshes: cerebellum-right, cerebellum-left, cerebellum-vermis): The striated hindbrain structure resting beneath the occipital cortex behind the fourth ventricle and pons. Function: Fine-tunes posture, balance, ocular tracking, and smooth motor execution through continuous sensory feedback.
    - Fact: Attached to the brainstem behind the pons, the cerebellum compares planned motor signals with proprioceptive feedback to coordinate smooth movement. [OpenStax, §13.2, 'The Cerebellum' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/13-2-the-central-nervous-system)]
    - Fact: Parallel surface ridges called folia fold the cerebellar cortex tightly above its deep white matter. [Encyclopaedia Britannica, Section 'Cerebellum' (https://www.britannica.com/science/human-brain)]
  - **Brainstem & spinal cord** (high confidence; meshes: brainstem, spinal-cord): The continuous ventral-posterior neural axis of midbrain, pons, medulla oblongata, and upper cervical spinal cord. Function: Controls vital respiratory and cardiovascular rhythms while conducting ascending sensory and descending motor tracts.
    - Fact: The midbrain, pons, and medulla oblongata form the brainstem, bridging the diencephalon and cerebellum with the spinal cord. [OpenStax, §13.2, 'The Brain Stem' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/13-2-the-central-nervous-system)]
    - Fact: Autonomic centres in the pons and medulla regulate breathing rhythm, heart rate, and vascular tone. [OpenStax, §35.3, 'Brain: Brainstem' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/35-3-the-central-nervous-system)]
